transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I’m only sitting in this chair because everybody keeps acting like I’m just imagining it. My wife, everybody... they look at me like I'm making it up. But I'm a fabricator, doc. I work with precision parts all day long for a living. I know exactly where things are supposed to be, down to the millimeter. And I know for an absolute fact that my wife’s relative has been coming into this house to get at me. 

It’s not a mistake, and I'm not seeing things. Tools don’t just move themselves. I have a very specific system in my garage. I'll put my torque wrench on the second shelf, facing left, right where it belongs. I come out the next morning, and it’s on the bottom shelf, facing right. Or my micrometers are taken out of their case and left on the workbench. He's coming in and messing with my stuff just to get under my skin, to make me doubt myself. 

And it’s not just the tools, either. Every single weekend, my fishing plans get completely spoiled, and it is never by accident. I'll have everything ready to go down to the lake—truck packed, bait sorted—and suddenly my good line is tangled to hell, or the latch on my boat trailer is mysteriously jammed with a piece of wire, or my tackle box has been dumped and reorganized all wrong. Every single weekend! 

It's been going on for months now, and nobody wants to listen to me. But I can see it plain as day. He’s been doing all this because he’s trying to take over my place. He wants to push me out of my own home, make me look like I'm losing my grip so he can just step in and take over my house and my life. And my wife just sighs and tells me I need to talk to a doctor, but if you saw the way he looks at my property, you'd know exactly what he's up to.
Have you heard or seen things that other people could not?

Look, if you're asking if I'm hearing voices whispering in the walls or seeing ghosts floating around the garage, no. Absolutely not. I'm not crazy, doc. I get my hearing checked every single year at the plant. It's a strict OSHA requirement, you know, because we work around heavy hydraulic presses and pneumatic riveters all day long, and you've got to wear your PPE, your earplugs, your muffs, so they test us annually. My hearing is perfectly fine for a fifty-four-year-old guy. 

And my eyes are fine too. I wear safety glasses on the floor, and I've got my reading glasses for the really fine micrometer work, but I don't see things that aren't there. That's the whole point I keep trying to get through my wife's head! I'm not imagining some phantom moving my stuff. I'm seeing real, solid, physical objects—heavy drop-forged steel tools—that have been picked up by a real human hand and moved to a completely different shelf. 

You can't hallucinate a jammed boat trailer latch. You can't just imagine a tangled spool of monofilament line. If you reach out and touch it, it's there. It's real, tangible evidence. So no, I'm not sitting here telling you I have magical visions or hear secret messages from the television. I'm telling you a flesh-and-blood guy is walking onto my property, breathing my air, and touching my things, plain as day.
Has anything happened to you that would be impossible in real life, like someone controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?

Look, doc, I don't know what kind of people you usually sit and talk to in here, but no. Nobody is beaming thoughts into my head or steering me around like some kind of remote-control car. That is sci-fi stuff. That is late-night television. I deal in the physical world. I told you, I work with precision parts. If a piece of 6061 aluminum is out of tolerance by three thousandths of an inch, it doesn't fit the assembly. It is just a fact. It is not magic, it is not mind control, it is a physical reality. 

My thoughts are entirely my own. I wake up at 4:30 every single morning, I make my coffee—black, no sugar, the exact same way I have for thirty years—and I think about the production schedule for the day. I think about my wife, I think about my house, and yeah, lately, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to catch this guy in the act. But those are my thoughts. I generated them in my own brain. I am reacting to a real, physical situation that is happening right in front of me. 

If someone comes into your garage and touches your tools, you don't need someone putting thoughts into your brain to get mad about it. You just get mad because it is your property! I bought that torque wrench in 1998, okay? It is a heavy-duty piece of equipment. You don't just let people mess with a tool like that. If you came into your clinic and found your stethoscope or your patient files all rearranged on your desk, you would immediately think to yourself that someone was in your office. You wouldn't sit there and wonder if someone was controlling your mind to make you upset. You would know a physical person walked in and messed with your stuff. 

That is exactly what I am dealing with. So no, nothing impossible is happening to me. No mind-reading, no telepathy, no secret mind-control rays. Just a very real, very sneaky guy trying to play games with my life and my property, and I am apparently the only one thinking clearly enough to see it for exactly what it is.
Before all this started, did you have any major medical illness or head injury?

No, doc, no. I haven't had any head injuries. I mean, you work on a factory floor for thirty-some years, you're going to get some bumps and scrapes, right? I've pinched my fingers in a press a few times, got a nice little scar on my left knuckle from a slip with a deburring tool back in '04, maybe '05. You get some metal shavings in your hands, you get a sore back from standing on concrete for ten hours a day. That's just the nature of the beast. But a head injury? Like a concussion or something? No, never. 

We wear hard hats in the designated zones, anyway. Safety first, right? They're always on us about safety. "Wear your PPE, watch your clearance, keep your area clean." So, no, nothing like that. No major medical stuff either. I've never had a heart attack, no strokes, no cancer, thank God. My blood pressure is a little high, maybe, but whose isn't these days? I take a pill for it, and it's fine. My cholesterol was up a bit a few years ago, so my wife got on this kick of making me eat oatmeal every morning instead of bacon and eggs. I hated it for a month, but I got used to it. Now I kind of like it. 

But no, I'm healthy as a horse. I haven't even had the flu in probably five years. I take my vitamins, I try to get enough sleep, even though I've been waking up a lot lately because I'm so worried about this guy coming around. But as far as some big medical problem or getting hit in the head with a wrench? No. My brain works perfectly fine, doc. Like I said, I'm not sick. I'm just dealing with a very real problem that nobody else seems to want to acknowledge.
How long have you believed that your wife’s relative has been coming into your house and moving your things?

Well, if you want to get down to brass tacks, it's been about nine months. Nine months of this absolute nonsense. And it is not a coincidence, doc, because that is exactly when my wife's relative moved into our home. 

You see, he had some sort of falling out with his landlord, or he couldn't make rent, or whatever the sob story was—my wife always has some excuse for him, always babying him. She comes to me and says, "Oh, he just needs a place to crash for a little bit, let's put him up in the spare room." I didn't want it. I told her right then and there, I said, look, I work ten, sometimes twelve-hour shifts on the factory floor. When I clock out and come back to my house, I want peace and quiet. I don't want a roommate at fifty-four years old. I've earned my space. But you know how it goes, you argue and argue, and eventually you just cave to keep the peace. So I let him move in. 

And I swear to you, almost the very first week he was living in our house, that's when the games started. That's when things started shifting around in the garage. Like I told you before, I keep a meticulous workspace. At the plant, we use the 5S system for organization—Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. Every single tool has a shadow board, every part has a labeled bin. I do the exact same thing at home. So if my three-eighths drive ratchet is sitting on the second shelf instead of hanging on its specific peg, I know it.
Since this started, have you had a period where you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?

Unusually energetic? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, look, I've always been a hard worker. You don't survive thirty-two years on a fabrication line by dragging your feet, right? You have to keep pace. The line doesn't stop because you're feeling sluggish. So I've always had a good motor on me, always been able to put in a solid day's work and then come home and mow the lawn or fix a leaky faucet or whatever needs doing. 

But as far as feeling, what did you call it, unusually energetic? No. If anything, I'm just running on pure adrenaline and frustration lately. And the sleep thing... well, like I mentioned a minute ago, my sleep hasn't been great, but it's not because I don't *need* sleep. Believe me, doc, at fifty-four, after standing on concrete all day, my body absolutely needs sleep. My back aches, my knees ache, my shoulders are tight. I want to sleep. I crave a solid eight hours. 

But I can't. Because how can you sleep when you know someone is creeping around your property, disrespecting your space, messing with the order of things? So I'll lay there in bed, staring at the ceiling fan, listening. Just listening to every little creak and groan the house makes. Is that the wind, or is that him out in the garage again? Did I hear the side door open? Did he leave a window unlatched? So I'll get up, put my slippers on, and go do a perimeter check. I check the locks, I check the garage, I make sure the motion sensor lights are working. 

By the time I get back to bed, I'm all wound up again. And then my alarm goes off at 4:30. So, no, I don't feel like I don't need sleep. I need it desperately. I'm exhausted, to be honest with you. I'm running on fumes some days. But I can't let my guard down, not even for a minute, because the second I do, that's when he'll strike. That's when he'll go in there and move my calipers or hide my socket set just to mess with my head. So, energetic? No. Just vigilant. Highly, highly vigilant.
Is your wife’s relative living in your house right now?

No! No, he's not. And that's exactly the point, doc! That's what I've been trying to tell everyone, but nobody wants to listen to me! I’m here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining it, like I'm crazy or something. My wife, her sister, even the guys at the plant—they all look at me like I've got two heads when I bring it up. But I know what's going on. I know my wife’s relative came into this house to get at me. 

He moved out, what, three months ago? Said he finally got on his feet and found a place across town. But you think that stopped him? Not a chance. If anything, it's worse now because he's sneaking around instead of just living down the hall. My tools don’t move themselves, doc! I already told you about the shadow boards and the 5S system. A wrench doesn't just sprout legs and walk from the pegboard to the workbench. And it's not just the tools anymore. 

It's my whole life! Every weekend, I try to go out to the lake. I've got a little aluminum boat, a 14-footer with a 9.9 Evinrude on the back. Nothing fancy, but it's mine, and I like to go out early on Saturday mornings and just cast a line, get some peace and quiet. But my fishing plans don’t get spoiled by accident every single weekend. One week, the trailer lights are suddenly shorted out. The next week, the spark plugs on the outboard are fouled. Last week, I go out to hook up the trailer, and the hitch pin is gone. Just gone! You don't just lose a heavy-duty steel hitch pin! He's doing it. He's coming around when we're asleep or when I'm at the plant, and he's sabotaging me. 

And I know why, too. It took me a while to piece it all together, but after all these months I can see plain as day he’s been trying to take over my place and push me out. He sees what I have—a good job, a nice house, a stable life—and he wants it. He wants to drive me out of my own home so he can just slide right in and take over. He's trying to make me look crazy to my wife so she'll kick me out and let him move back in permanently. But I'm not going to let it happen. I've worked too hard for thirty-two years to just hand over everything I've built to some freeloader who can't even pay his own rent!
Has anyone told you that your speech has become hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another?

Hard to follow? Jump from one idea to... no. No, absolutely not. If anything, I'm the only one making any sense around here. 

I speak very plainly, doc. I mean, look at what I do for a living. You don't work on a fabrication line by being all over the place. Everything is sequential. You follow the schematic. You go from step one to step two to step three. If you're training a new guy on the press brake and you start jumping around with your instructions, somebody is going to lose a hand. You have to be precise. You have to be clear. And that's exactly how I am in my everyday life. 

So, no, nobody has ever told me my speech is hard to follow. I lay things out logically. I lay out the facts. The problem—and this is what really, really gets under my skin—the problem isn't that I'm hard to follow, it's that they don't *want* to follow it. My wife, for instance, she hears me explain exactly how the timeline matches up, how the missing hitch pin connects to him wanting me out of the house, and she just... she rolls her eyes. She tunes me out. 

It's like I'm laying out a perfectly good blueprint right in front of her on the kitchen table, showing her exactly what's happening, and she refuses to look at it because looking at it would mean admitting her precious relative is a snake. It's easier for them to act like I'm the one not making sense than to face the truth. But my mind is sharp, doc. I don't jump around. I stay entirely focused on the facts. I have to stay focused, because if I lose my train of thought or let myself get distracted for even a second, that's when he gets the upper hand. So no, I make perfect sense. It's everyone else who's refusing to connect the dots.
Have you ever called the police or set up a camera to catch him coming into your house?

The police? Call the police for what? "Excuse me, officer, my 10-millimeter socket is in the wrong drawer and my boat trailer lights are shorted out"? They’d laugh me right out of the precinct. They want a smoking gun, doc. They don't care about the... the slow, methodical sabotage of a man's garage. And cameras, well, I looked into those trail cams, the motion-activated ones they sell over at Cabela's, but I haven't set one up yet because I know he'd just find a blind spot or steal the camera itself. 

So instead, I’ve just had to completely change how I operate in my own space. I mean, I’ve stopped leaving my equipment where I used to. It used to be, I’d be working on rebuilding a small engine or something, and I could just leave my tools out on the bench overnight so I could pick right back up the next day. Not anymore. Now, everything goes back in the heavy-duty steel chest. I bought three new hardened-steel Master Locks, and I spend a lot of time—probably too much time, if you ask my wife—just locking things up and checking the workshop. I'll go out there three, four times an evening just to physically pull on the padlocks and make sure the window latches haven't been jimmied. 

And when he actually has the nerve to come over—because my wife still invites him back to the house
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Lost interest? No, no, I haven't lost interest. I just told you, I still try to go out to the lake every single weekend! I want to fish. I love fishing. I've loved fishing since my old man took me out for crappie when I was eight years old. I've got that 14-foot aluminum boat, the Evinrude... I keep my tackle box organized, I tie my own jigs, I do all of it. I have the interest. I have all the interest in the world! 

It's just that I can't actually *enjoy* it anymore, or even get out on the water half the time, because I'm constantly having to deal with the sabotage. How are you supposed to enjoy a peaceful Saturday morning on the water when you're spending two hours in the driveway trying to figure out why the trailer lights are completely dead, tracing wires, looking for the short he deliberately caused? You can't. The joy just gets sucked right out of it. 

And my workshop, same thing. I love working with my hands. I love fixing small engines, building things, keeping everything shipshape. But now, instead of just walking out there, flipping on the shop light, and getting into the flow of the work, I'm doing a full security sweep. I'm checking the Master Locks, I'm inspecting the window latches, I'm doing inventory on my shadow boards to see what he moved or took while I was sleeping. I still want to do my projects, doc. I really do. But it's turned into a full-time job just protecting my things from him. 

So it's not that I don't care about my hobbies anymore. I haven't lost interest at all. I'm just... I'm exhausted from having to defend my life, my home, my boat, everything I've worked for, against a guy who's actively trying to ruin it all. If he would just leave me alone, stop sneaking in, stop messing with my gear, I'd be out on that lake right now casting for bass and having the time of my life. But he won't let me.
During these past nine months, have you had a period of feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? Like, clinically depressed? No, doc, no. I mean, I'm not sitting around crying into my coffee or staring at the wall all day. I get up, I go to work, I punch the clock, I do my job on the line. I come home, I check the locks, I check the boat trailer, I make sure the garage hasn't been compromised. I'm active. I'm vigilant. You can't be vigilant if you're depressed and just, you know, giving up on everything. 

Now, am I frustrated? Absolutely. Am I angry? You bet your life I am. I mean, wouldn't you be? If you spent nine months—almost a whole year, doc—having to constantly look over your shoulder in your own home? Having to check the tension on your window latches every single night before you can even think about going to sleep? Having your own wife look at you like you're the one with the problem while her relative is actively dismantling your peace of mind piece by piece? It takes a toll, I'm not going to lie to you about that. It wears a man down. 

There are days when I pull into the driveway after a ten-hour shift on the floor, and my shoulders just slump because I know before I even put the truck in park that I've got to do a full perimeter sweep. I know I'm going to walk into that garage and find my torque wrench moved two inches to the left, just to mess with my head. That's exhausting. It's draining. Sometimes I just want to sit in the cab of my truck for ten minutes with the radio off just to have a moment of peace before the battle starts again. 

But depressed? No. I don't feel hopeless. I don't feel sad. I feel targeted. And when you're being targeted, you don't have time to be depressed. You have to stay sharp. You have to stay angry, honestly, because that anger is what keeps you focused on protecting what's yours. If I let myself get depressed, if I just threw my hands up and said, "Woe is me," he'd win. He'd have the run of the place. He'd probably have my boat sold for scrap by now. So no, I haven't been depressed. I've just been pushed to my absolute limit by a situation that nobody else seems to want to acknowledge.
Have you started using methamphetamine, cocaine, or any new medication or drug around the time this began?

Drugs? Are you kidding me, doc? Meth? Cocaine? Look at me. Do I look like some junkie tweaking out behind a gas station? I'm fifty-four years old. I've been working on the assembly line for almost thirty years. You don't keep a job fabricating sheet metal and running heavy machinery if you're hopped up on speed. They do random urinalysis at the plant, for crying out loud. If you so much as drop a pallet jack too hard or bump a forklift into a safety rail, HR sends you straight down to the occupational clinic to pee in a cup. I'd have been fired twenty years ago if I messed around with garbage like that. 

I don't take anything. No new medications, no illegal drugs, nothing. I haven't even changed my brand of toothpaste. I drink my Folgers in the morning, black, and maybe, just maybe, I'll have a Miller Lite on a Saturday if I'm out in the yard pulling weeds, but that is the extent of my chemical intake. 

It honestly... it kind of offends me that you'd even ask that, but I guess I get it. You're a psychiatrist, you have to check the boxes on your clipboard. You're looking for a chemical reason for why I'm so wound up. You think maybe I'm hallucinating the scratches on my Master Locks because I'm on a bender? Or that I'm imagining the wiring on my boat trailer being stripped because I took some bad pills? 

No. No, doc, I'm completely sober. The only thing keeping me awake at night isn't methamphetamine, it's him. It's the constant, undeniable fact that someone is sneaking onto my property. You don't need drugs to be on edge when someone is actually out to get you. I've got a completely clear head, 100 percent sober, and that's exactly why I'm the only one who can see exactly what he's doing while my wife and everyone else just turn a blind eye. So no, no drugs. Just a guy trying to protect his own house.
Aside from dealing with this situation, have you become less emotionally expressive or more withdrawn from other people?

Withdrawn? Less emotionally expressive? No, I... look, I don't know who told you that, maybe my wife said something, but no. I'm the exact same guy I've always been. I still get up at 4:30 every single morning, I pack my thermos, and I go down to the plant. I do my assembler work, same as I have for almost thirty years. You can't be withdrawn on the fabrication floor, doc. You have to communicate. You're working with heavy sheets of steel, you're shouting over the noise of the hydraulic presses, you're coordinating with the guys on the line—you have to be engaged. I still joke around with the guys in the breakroom, I still talk about the football game on Mondays. I'm expressing myself just fine.

I keep the bills paid, and I take care of myself like I always have. The mortgage check goes out on the first of the month, every month, without fail. The electric bill gets paid, I keep the truck's oil changed, I shower, I shave, I eat my meals. I'm not hiding under the covers or shutting down. I'm functioning exactly like a normal, responsible adult is supposed to function. 

The trouble... the only trouble here is all centered on what’s happening in my house with him and my things. That's it. That is the entire issue. So if I seem a little quiet when I get home, or if my wife thinks I'm not sitting on the couch making enough small talk about the neighbor's new landscaping, it's not because my emotions are shut off or because I'm withdrawing from her. It's because I'm listening. I'm sitting there at the kitchen table, and I'm straining to hear the squeak of the side gate. I'm waiting to hear if he's out there messing with the padlock on my shed again or tampering with the boat trailer. 

You can't just kick back and chat about nothing when you know your property is actively being messed with. You have to be alert. You have to be on guard. So, sure, maybe to someone who completely refuses to see what's really going on, it looks like I'm pulling away or getting quiet. But I'm not withdrawn. I'm just focused. I have to be the one paying attention, because nobody else in that house will.
Have you been having problems with your memory lately?

Memory? No, no, my memory is... honestly, doc, my memory is probably the only thing keeping me from completely going under with everything happening around my own house. If I had memory problems, this guy would have me convinced I was the one making mistakes by now. He'd absolutely love that, wouldn't he? If I just started forgetting where I put things, he could just run roughshod over my entire property and I'd never be the wiser. 

But no, my memory is like a steel trap. I have to remember every single detail. When I put my tools away in the garage after a shift, I don't just toss them in the chest. I set them down in a very specific order. I know exactly how many threads are showing on the mounting bolts of my boat trailer winch. I count them, doc. Four threads showing on the left side, three on the right. If I go out there tomorrow morning before work and there are five threads showing, I know for a fact he's been out there with a socket wrench while I was sleeping. You can't keep track of things like that if your memory is slipping. I remember the exact angle I leave the padlock hanging on the shed door. I remember the exact pitch of the squeak the side gate makes when it latches—it has this very specific metallic click, and if it sounds dull or muffled, I know someone has been tampering with the strike plate. 

So no, my memory is perfectly fine. In fact, it's sharper than it's ever been in my entire fifty-four years on this earth because it has to be. Now, my wife, she might try to tell you I'm forgetting things. She'll get on my case and complain that I forgot to pick up milk on the way home, or that I forgot we were supposed to call her sister or something. But that's not a memory problem. That's just... that's just a matter of priorities. How am I supposed to remember to buy a gallon of two-percent milk when I'
If your wife showed you clear proof that no one had entered the house, would you believe her?

Proof? What... what kind of proof could she possibly have? A video camera that just happened to be pointing the wrong way? Or some timeline she wrote down? You can't prove a negative, doc. Especially not when the physical evidence is staring you right in the face every single morning. 

I mean, look, I know exactly why I’m sitting here in this office. I’m here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining it. My wife, her family, probably you now—you all look at me like I'm
Has he ever done something to you that would be impossible in real life?

Impossible? Like... like magic or something? No, no, doc, that's... that's exactly the problem here. There's nothing impossible about what he's doing. If he was walking through walls or turning invisible, then yeah, maybe I'd say, "Okay, I need to get my head checked." But he's not doing anything impossible. He's just... he's just incredibly careful, and he's got the time to do it. 

He's a flesh-and-blood guy. He uses tools. He uses leverage. He uses patience. That's what makes it so maddening! When I find the mounting bolts on my boat trailer tampered with, it's not because a ghost did it. It's because a guy with a half-inch socket wrench came into my yard, probably wearing dark clothes, probably keeping low behind the hedges by the driveway, and he put in the physical work to mess with my property. When the side gate latch is slightly bent, it's because someone applied physical force to it. 

There's no hocus-pocus here. It's all real, tangible stuff. He's picking locks, he's unscrewing hinges, he's moving my tools an inch to the left just to mess with my head. That's all completely possible for a guy who knows what he's doing and has the time to wait until I'm asleep or at the plant. He knows my schedule, doc. He knows I leave for the plant at 4:30 AM. He knows I'm gone for eight, sometimes ten hours if we're pushing a quota on the fabrication floor. That's a huge window of time for a guy to slip in, do his damage, and slip out without doing anything "impossible." 

So no, he hasn't done anything impossible. He's just... he's just very, very good at being sneaky, and he's exploiting the fact that my wife refuses to see what's right in front of her. If it was impossible, I wouldn't be sitting here trying to convince you it's real. I'd be trying to figure out how a guy walks through a solid oak door. But he doesn't. He just picks the lock.
Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your actions?

Controlling my actions? Like... like making me do things? Like a puppet on a string or something? No, no, doc, absolutely not. I am in complete control of what I do. Every move I make is my own. When I clock in at the fabrication floor, my hands are doing exactly what my brain tells them to do. I'm the one measuring the steel, I'm the one operating the press, I'm the one driving my truck home. Nobody is pulling my strings. 

If someone was literally controlling my actions, I mean, think about it—why wouldn't this guy just make me leave the garage door wide open for him? Why would he bother with the half-inch socket wrench and picking the padlock on the shed if he could just, I don't know, beam a thought into my head and make me hand him the keys? It doesn't make any sense. He has to do things the hard way because I am fully in the driver's seat of my own body, and I make sure everything is locked down tight. 

Now, if you want to get technical about it, you could say he's dictating my schedule, sure. He's forcing my hand in that way, because now I have to spend an extra forty-five minutes every single morning just walking the perimeter of my property before I even pour my coffee. I have to start at the front porch, check the weatherstripping on the main door, then I move down the driveway to the side gate—the one with the squeak I told you about—then I check the garage, the shed, the boat trailer. I do all of that because I have to, because of him. So he's changing my routine, yeah. He's making me have to be vigilant. But he's not literally moving my arms and legs. I choose to get up at 3:45 AM to do that perimeter check. I choose to count the threads on those bolts. I'm fully in control of myself, doc. It's my property I can't control, because this guy refuses to stay off it.
Has anyone shown you definite evidence that your tools or boat problems had an ordinary explanation, and you still felt sure he did it?

Evidence? You mean like when my wife tries to tell me the wind knocked over the sawhorses, or that I must have just misplaced my own socket set? Yeah, she tries that all the time. She’ll say, "Oh, honey, you just forgot where you put the drill," or "The boat trailer was just sitting out in the rain, that’s why it’s rusty." 

But doc, come on. I’ve been working with tools since I was a teenager. I’m a fabricator, for crying out loud. I know exactly where I put my tools down. I know how tight I torque a bolt. And the wind doesn't unlatch a heavy-duty padlock and then latch it back up again, does it? The rain doesn't systematically move my crescent wrenches out of size order. 

I mean, that’s exactly why I’m here, isn't it? I’m here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining it, but I know my wife’s relative came into this house to get at me. It's him. It's her brother, or her cousin, or whoever she's got doing this dirty work. Because my tools don’t move themselves. My fishing plans don’t get spoiled by accident every single weekend. Every time I plan to take the boat out to the reservoir, suddenly there's a problem with the hitch, or the battery is drained, or the spark plugs are fouled. Every time. It honestly... it kind of offends me that you'd even ask that, but I guess I get it. You're a psychiatrist, you have to check the boxes on your clipboard. You're looking for a chemical reason for why I'm so wound up. You think maybe I'm hallucinating the scratches on my Master Locks because I'm on a bender? No. No, doc, I'm completely sober. The only thing keeping me awake at night isn't methamphetamine, it's him. It's the constant, undeniable fact that someone is sneaking onto my property. patient.answer:
Withdrawn? Less emotionally expressive? No, I... look, I don't know who told you that, maybe my wife said something, but no. I'm the exact same guy I've always been. You can't be withdrawn on the fabrication floor, doc. You have to communicate. I still joke around with the guys in the breakroom, I still talk about the football game on Mondays. I'm expressing myself just fine.

The trouble... the only trouble here is all centered on what’s happening in my house with him and my things. That's it. That is the entire issue. So if I seem a little quiet when I get home, or if my wife thinks I'm not sitting on the couch making enough small talk about the neighbor's new landscaping, it's not because my emotions are shut off or because I'm withdrawing from her. I have to be the one paying attention, because nobody else in that house will.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusional belief is bizarre/impossible versus a plausible persecutory delusion, to distinguish schizophrenia or acute polymorphic psychosis from persistent delusional disorder/organic delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Has he ever done something to you that would be impossible in real life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about bizarre delusions (something impossible in real life), which is not explicitly covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Impossible? Like... like magic or something? No, no, doc, that's... that's exactly the problem here. There's nothing impossible about what he's doing. If he was walking through walls or turning invisible, then yeah, maybe I'd say, "Okay, I need to get my head checked." But he's not doing anything impossible. He's just... he's just incredibly careful, and he's got the time to do it. 

He's a flesh-and-blood guy. He uses tools. He uses leverage. He uses patience. That's what makes it so maddening! There's no hocus-pocus here. It's all real, tangible stuff. He's picking locks, he's unscrewing hinges, he's moving my tools an inch to the left just to mess with my head. Now, if you want to get technical about it, you could say he's dictating my schedule, sure. patient.answer:
Evidence? You mean like when my wife tries to tell me the wind knocked over the sawhorses, or that I must have just misplaced my own socket set? Yeah, she tries that all the time. She’ll say, "Oh, honey, you just forgot where you put the drill," or "The boat trailer was just sitting out in the rain, that’s why it’s rusty." 

But doc, come on. I’ve been working with tools since I was a teenager. I’m a fabricator, for crying out loud. I know exactly where I put my tools down. I know how tight I torque a bolt. And the wind doesn't unlatch a heavy-duty padlock and then latch it back up again, does it? The rain doesn't systematically move my crescent wrenches out of size order. 

I mean, that’s exactly why I’m here, isn't it? I’m here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining it, but I know my wife’s relative came into this house to get at me. It's him. It's her brother, or her cousin, or whoever she's got doing this dirty work. Because my tools don’t move themselves. My fishing plans don’t get spoiled by accident every single weekend. Every time I plan to take the boat out to the reservoir, suddenly there's a problem with the hitch, or the battery is drained, or the spark plugs are fouled. Every time. That's not a coincidence, doc. That's a pattern. 

And after all these months of this happening, day in and day out, week after week... I can see plain as day he’s been trying to take over my place and push me out. He wants me to look crazy. He wants my wife to think I'm losing my mind so she'll kick me out and he can just waltz right in and take over everything I've built. The house, the garage, the boat. All of it. So yeah, they show me their "ordinary explanations," but I know better. I know exactly what's going on. They can't pull the wool over my eyes, no matter how many times they tell me it was just the wind.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been any other psychotic symptoms beyond the fixed persecutory delusion, especially bizarre delusions, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia.

patient.answer:
Other beliefs? Look, doc, I gotta stop you right there because... well, calling it a "belief" makes it sound like I'm sitting around talking about Bigfoot or UFOs or, I don't know, the government putting microchips in the water supply. No. No, I don't have any "other beliefs" because I don't even consider *this* a belief. It's not a belief. It's a fact. It's just what's actually happening on my property. 

I'm a practical guy. You ask anybody down at the plant. You ask my shift manager. He'll tell you. He'll say, "He's a straight shooter, he comes in, he does his work, he checks his tolerances." I deal in tangible things, doc. Steel. Aluminum. If a piece of metal is off by a sixteenth of an inch on the press, the whole assembly gets kicked back by quality control. You can't just *believe* a piece of steel into fitting. It either fits or it doesn't. My whole life, my whole career for the last thirty-some years, is based on what's right in front of me. What I can measure with a caliper. What I can touch with my own two hands. 

There's guys at the shop, sure, they talk about all kinds of crazy stuff in the breakroom. Fake moon landings, secret societies, whatever they saw on the internet the night before. I don't pay any attention to that garbage. I read the local paper, I check the weather report so I know if I need to tarp the boat, and that's it. I don't have time for fairy tales. 

So no, I don't have any other... whatever you want to call them. I don't think the CIA is tapping my phone. I don't think the neighbors are spying on me—well, except for the fact that they probably see him sneaking around my side gate and just don't want to get involved, which is a whole other issue with people these days, nobody wants to look out for their community anymore, everybody just minds their own business even when a guy is getting robbed blind. But I'm not making up wild stories. I just want to go to work, put in my hours, come home, maybe take the boat out to the reservoir on a Sunday, and be left alone. That's it. That's my whole worldview. 

The only problem, the *only* thing going on, is this guy, her relative, actively trespassing and trying to ruin my life so he can take my house. That's not a belief. That's a home invasion in slow motion. If he wasn't doing this, I wouldn't be sitting in this chair talking to you. I'd be out in the garage right now. So no, nothing else. Just the facts of what he's doing to me.
